findings.topic: Empty / unset HMAC key = universal forgery (the open door, still open)
findings.answer: ATTACK: apollo_wa_hmac_key defaults to '' and is only generated when an admin saves Tela 1 — never on activation. If verify() computes hash_hmac('sha512', $raw, '') against a fresh install, the key is the empty string, which every attacker knows. Anyone can sign any body and the route authenticates them. Same class of hole if the option holds a short/placeholder value. DEFENCE: read the key once, reject before any hashing when it is not a string, is shorter than the registry's hmac_min_bytes (32), or is empty; return the same opaque 401 as a bad signature. MISTAKE THAT INTRODUCES IT: `$key = (string) Apollo_Waha_Options::get('apollo_wa_hmac_key'); if (hash_equals(hash_hmac('sha512',$raw,$key), $sig))` with no emptiness gate — the code 'works' in the lab because the operator saved Tela 1, and ships open on every fresh site.
findings.evidence: inc/class-options.php:26 DEFAULTS['apollo_wa_hmac_key'] => ''; admin/class-admin.php:128-129 generates it only inside the Tela 1 admin-post handler; registry security.hmac_min_bytes=32; route is registered unconditionally at inc/Webhook/class-webhook.php:24-34.
findings.code_guidance: $key = Apollo_Waha_Options::get('apollo_wa_hmac_key', ''); if (!is_string($key) || strlen($key) < 32) { return $this->deny(); } // never hash_hmac with a short/empty key, never report 'key not configured' to the caller

findings.topic: Forged / unsigned events — every fail-open shape of the signature gate
findings.answer: ATTACK: the docs' headline threat — anyone POSTs a `message` or `session.status` body and the plugin acts on it. Fail-open variants: signature checked only `if header present`; permission_callback => __return_true; falling back to is_user_logged_in()/current_user_can(); verifying in handle() but leaving permission_callback true; accepting when hash_hmac() returns false/'' after an internal error; `try { verify } catch (\Throwable) { return true; }`. DEFENCE: single fail-closed funnel — every path that is not a fully-verified request returns the identical 401; the default of every branch is deny; the signature check is unconditional and lives in permission_callback so WP cannot dispatch handle() without it. MISTAKE: `if ($sig !== null && !hash_equals(...)) return false; return true;` — a missing header skips the whole check.
findings.evidence: docs/WEBHOOK-SECURITY.md:7-9 ('never "if header present"'), :45 (permission_callback = verify, not is_user_logged_in), :78 (__return_true = core 12-point fail); registry webhook.pipeline[2] 'require-hmac-header-401'; registry security.fail_closed=true.
findings.code_guidance: Structure verify() as: gather → validate → `return true` exactly once at the bottom; every other exit is `return $this->deny()`. No boolean accumulator variable, no early `return true`.

findings.topic: Algorithm confusion — never feed X-Webhook-Hmac-Algorithm into hash_hmac()
findings.answer: ATTACK: attacker sends `X-Webhook-Hmac-Algorithm: crc32b` (or md5/adler32) and a digest computed with that cheap algorithm. If the header is passed through to hash_hmac() as the algo argument, the server validates the attacker's own choice — trivially forgeable without the key. Variant: attacker sends an unsupported algo and PHP 8 throws ValueError → uncaught → 500 with a stack trace instead of 401. DEFENCE: the algorithm is a hardcoded literal 'sha512'; the header is only an allowlist gate compared with a strict string compare and nothing else. MISTAKE: `hash_hmac($request->get_header('x_webhook_hmac_algorithm'), $raw, $key)`, or `in_array($algo, $allowed)` (loose) instead of `'sha512' === $algo`.
findings.evidence: docs/WEBHOOK-SECURITY.md:50 'Algorithm allowlist: only sha512. Else 401'; :21 the signed value is hex(HMAC_SHA512(key, raw_body)); registry webhook.headers['X-Webhook-Hmac-Algorithm'] = 'sha512 only'.
findings.code_guidance: $algo = $request->get_header('x_webhook_hmac_algorithm'); if (!is_string($algo) || 'sha512' !== strtolower(trim($algo))) { return $this->deny(); } $calc = hash_hmac('sha512', $raw, $key); // literal, always

findings.topic: Timing attack on digest comparison — why ==, ===, strcmp and substr all fail
findings.answer: ATTACK: byte-by-byte comparators short-circuit on the first differing byte, so response time correlates with how many leading hex chars are right. An attacker who can send many requests recovers the 128-char digest for a chosen body one nibble at a time, then replays that body forever without ever knowing the key. `==` is additionally catastrophic on hex-looking strings in older semantics and still wrong here because it invites type juggling (PHP 8.3 no longer juggles numeric strings against non-numeric, but `0 == ''`-class surprises and array/null operands remain); `strcmp`/`strncmp`/`substr($a,0,8)===substr($b,0,8)` are all early-exit or truncating. DEFENCE: hash_equals(), which compares the full length in constant time and returns false immediately only on a length mismatch (leaking length only, which is fixed at 128 hex chars anyway). Do not add your own `strlen()` pre-check or a `substr` fast path in front of it — that reintroduces the oracle. Keep argument order known-first, user-second. MISTAKE: `if ($calc === $sig)`, or `if (strcmp($calc,$sig) === 0)`, or 'optimising' with a length guard before hash_equals.
findings.evidence: docs/WEBHOOK-SECURITY.md:51 'vs header via hash_equals'; :77 'Compare HMAC with === → use hash_equals'; registry security.compare = 'hash_equals'; audit checklist :107.
findings.code_guidance: $sig = $request->get_header('x_webhook_hmac'); if (!is_string($sig)) { return $this->deny(); } $sig = strtolower(trim($sig)); if (1 !== preg_match('/^[0-9a-f]{128}$/', $sig)) { return $this->deny(); } if (!hash_equals($calc, $sig)) { return $this->deny(); }

findings.topic: hash_equals(null, …) and array headers — TypeError becomes a 500 stack trace, not a 401
findings.answer: ATTACK: omit X-Webhook-Hmac entirely. WP_REST_Request::get_header() returns null for an absent header, and PHP 8.3 hash_equals() throws TypeError on a non-string argument. Uncaught inside permission_callback that is a fatal 500; with WP_DEBUG/display_errors on it prints a stack trace whose frames can carry the raw body and, depending on how the call is written, the key itself. So the simplest attack (send nothing) yields both the wrong status code and an information leak. Same for `$request->get_header_as_array()` (array) and for duplicate headers (WP implodes them with ',' — safe but never an array). DEFENCE: is_string() on every header before touching it; shape-validate the hex; never let a Throwable escape verify()/handle(). MISTAKE: trusting the type of `$request->get_header(...)` because 'WAHA always sends it'.
findings.evidence: WP_REST_Request::get_header() returns null when absent, otherwise implode(',', $values); docs/WEBHOOK-SECURITY.md:49 'Missing X-Webhook-Hmac → 401, log, stop'; :102 '401 must not leak'.
findings.code_guidance: Wrap the body of verify() in try { … } catch (\Throwable $e) { return $this->deny(); } and log only $e->getMessage() behind WP_DEBUG — never $raw, never $key, never $calc.

findings.topic: permission_callback returning bare false yields 403 for logged-in callers, not the specified 401
findings.answer: ATTACK/FAILURE: WP turns a `false` from permission_callback into WP_Error('rest_forbidden', …, ['status' => rest_authorization_required_code()]) — that helper returns 401 for anonymous callers but 403 when a valid auth cookie is present. An admin's browser (or a CSRF'd admin session from evil.com) POSTing the webhook therefore gets 403, contradicting the status table, and the difference between 401 and 403 becomes an oracle telling the attacker whether their cookie was recognised — i.e. the response distinguishes 'who you are' on a route that must be identity-blind. DEFENCE: never return bare false; always return an explicit WP_Error with array('status' => 401) so the code is constant regardless of cookie state. MISTAKE: keeping the stub's `return false;` shape (inc/Webhook/class-webhook.php:37) as the deny path.
findings.evidence: inc/Webhook/class-webhook.php:36-38 current `verify()` returns false; docs/WEBHOOK-SECURITY.md:96 'Auth fail (no/bad hmac, bad algo, stale ts, bad session) → 401'; registry rest.routes.webhook.cookie_auth=false.
findings.code_guidance: private function deny(): WP_Error { return new WP_Error('apollo_wa_webhook_denied', 'Unauthorized', array('status' => 401)); } // identical object for every auth failure; message never varies

findings.topic: Replay: the timestamp and Request-Id are OUTSIDE the MAC, so neither is a real replay defence
findings.answer: ATTACK (design-level, easy to miss): the signature covers the raw body only — hex(HMAC_SHA512(key, raw_body)). X-Webhook-Timestamp and X-Webhook-Request-Id are unauthenticated headers. An attacker who captures one legitimately signed body (proxy log, egress capture, a mirrored request, a leaked access log) can resend it indefinitely: rewrite the timestamp to now to pass the 300s window, and rewrite the Request-Id to a fresh random value to miss the dedupe transient. Both 'defences' are attacker-controlled. Replay inside the window is thus trivial and replay outside the window is equally trivial. DEFENCE: derive the idempotency key from signed material — prefer an id inside the verified payload (payload.id / message id / session.status sequence), and fall back to hash('sha256', $raw) so the same bytes can never be processed twice regardless of header games; if you also honour the header id, treat it as a hint that is combined with, never a substitute for, the body hash. Where the payload carries its own timestamp inside the signed body, prefer it over the header for the 300s window. Treat the header window as spam-shedding only, never as authentication. MISTAKE: 'the timestamp check stops replay' — it stops nothing an attacker who can edit a header cannot undo; keying the transient solely on X-Webhook-Request-Id makes dedupe opt-in for the attacker.
findings.evidence: docs/WEBHOOK-SECURITY.md:21 signature input is raw_body only; :52-53 window + Request-Id transient; :87-88 'HMAC does not cover: replay inside 5 min → Request-Id transient'; registry webhook.pipeline[5]/[6].
findings.code_guidance: $fingerprint = hash('sha256', $raw); $hdr_id = $request->get_header('x_webhook_request_id'); $id = (is_string($hdr_id) && 1 === preg_match('/^[A-Za-z0-9._:-]{1,64}$/', $hdr_id)) ? $hdr_id : substr($fingerprint, 0, 32); $key = 'apollo_wa_hook_' . $id; // and additionally guard on 'apollo_wa_hook_' . substr($fingerprint,0,32) so a rewritten header cannot re-open the door

findings.topic: Retry-vs-replay confusion — marking seen too early silently drops events; TOCTOU double-processes them
findings.answer: ATTACK/FAILURE: two symmetric bugs. (a) Set the transient before running the handler, then the handler 500s: WAHA retries, the retry hits the dedupe and gets 200-empty, and the event is lost forever with a success code — a silent availability failure an attacker can force by making a handler fail once. (b) get_transient() then set_transient() is not atomic: two concurrent WAHA retries both read 'not seen' and both process. For this run's session.status that is harmless, but the same code shape later governs message handling and anything that sends. DEFENCE: claim atomically at the start so concurrency is covered, and release the claim if the handler fails so a retry can proceed, returning 500 so WAHA retries; only a successful handler leaves the 10-minute marker. Handlers stay idempotent regardless. MISTAKE: `if (get_transient($k)) return 200; ... set_transient($k, 1, 600); process();` — wrong on both counts.
findings.evidence: docs/WEBHOOK-SECURITY.md:53 'Transient apollo_wa_hook_{Request-Id} TTL 10 min. Repeat → 200 empty'; :88 'WAHA retry after add already done'; :100 '500 (WAHA will retry — handlers must be idempotent)'; registry webhook.pipeline[6].
findings.code_guidance: if (false !== get_transient($k)) { return new WP_REST_Response(null, 200); } set_transient($k, 1, 10 * MINUTE_IN_SECONDS); try { $this->dispatch($data); } catch (\Throwable $e) { delete_transient($k); return new WP_REST_Response(array('ok'=>false), 500); }

findings.topic: Transient key built from an unsanitised Request-Id — option-name truncation, collision, and global event loss
findings.answer: ATTACK: X-Webhook-Request-Id is attacker-controlled text concatenated into a WordPress option name. (a) Length: wp_options.option_name is VARCHAR(191) and the '_transient_timeout_' prefix eats 19 chars, leaving 172; 'apollo_wa_hook_' eats 15 more. A >157-char id makes the timeout row and the value row truncate to different keys — the transient never expires correctly or never reads back, and dedupe silently stops working. (b) Collision: two long ids sharing a prefix truncate to the same row, so a legitimate event is dropped as a replay. (c) Empty/missing id: `'apollo_wa_hook_' . ''` becomes one shared key — the first event ever received poisons the next 10 minutes and every subsequent event returns 200-empty and is discarded. That is a one-request, unauthenticated-if-you-have-any-valid-body denial of the whole webhook. (d) Newlines/null bytes in the id land in log lines (log injection) and in option names. DEFENCE: allowlist-regex and length-cap the id; hash anything that does not match; never allow the empty case to produce a bare prefix. MISTAKE: `set_transient('apollo_wa_hook_' . $request->get_header('x_webhook_request_id'), 1, 600)`.
findings.evidence: docs/WEBHOOK-SECURITY.md:53; registry webhook.transient_prefix = 'apollo_wa_hook_'; wp_options.option_name is 191 chars, transient timeout prefix 19.
findings.code_guidance: preg_match('/^[A-Za-z0-9._:-]{1,64}$/', $hdr_id) or fall back to substr(hash('sha256',$raw),0,32); assert the final key length stays under 100 chars.

findings.topic: Body-size / compute DoS, and the ordering trap in the pipeline
findings.answer: ATTACK: unauthenticated POST of a 200 MB body. The pipeline lists body-max-256kb at position 9, after hash_hmac at position 5 — implemented literally, every attacker forces a SHA-512 over hundreds of MB plus a full copy in PHP memory before the size check ever runs. Repeat concurrently and PHP-FPM children exhaust memory. Variant: trusting Content-Length (a header the attacker writes, and which can disagree with the bytes delivered) instead of the actual string length. Variant: mb_strlen() under an overloaded mbstring counts characters, not bytes, so a multibyte body slips past a 262144 'byte' cap. DEFENCE: measure strlen() of the raw string the instant it is read, before hash_hmac, and bail there; keep the documented status semantics (413 for oversize) while never hashing an oversized body. Real hard limits belong upstream too (php post_max_size, nginx client_max_body_size) — the PHP check is the last line, not the first. MISTAKE: `$raw = file_get_contents('php://input'); $calc = hash_hmac('sha512',$raw,$key); … if (strlen($raw) > 262144) return 413;`
findings.evidence: docs/WEBHOOK-SECURITY.md:55 'Body > 256 KB → 413'; :48 'Raw body: file_get_contents(php://input). JSON parse AFTER verify'; registry webhook.pipeline[8] 'body-max-256kb-413'; status table :97.
findings.code_guidance: $raw = (string) file_get_contents('php://input'); if (strlen($raw) > 262144) { return new WP_Error('apollo_wa_webhook_large', 'Payload too large', array('status' => 413)); } // strlen(), binary-safe, before any hashing; never (int) $_SERVER['CONTENT_LENGTH']

findings.topic: JSON parse bombs, depth, and the deserialisation family
findings.answer: ATTACK: after the size cap the remaining parse risks are (a) depth — 256 KB of '[[[[…' costs recursion; PHP's default depth 512 makes json_decode return null rather than crash, but code that then does `$data['session']` on null emits warnings and, if the null path isn't handled, reaches handlers with no data; (b) wide objects — hundreds of thousands of keys inflating to a large PHP array; (c) invalid UTF-8 returning null; (d) the genuinely dangerous cousin: ever passing body bytes to unserialize()/maybe_unserialize() (PHP object injection / POP chain to RCE) or to extract() (variable overwrite) or to any eval/`create_function`/dynamic-callable path. DEFENCE: json_decode with assoc=true, an explicit low depth, JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR inside try/catch returning the opaque deny; then is_array() before any key access; no unserialize, no extract, no variable-variables, no raw SQL built from body values. MISTAKE: `$data = json_decode($raw, true); switch ($data['event'])` — null-deref warnings, and a 500 for malformed JSON where WAHA will then retry forever.
findings.evidence: docs/WEBHOOK-SECURITY.md:56 'Then switch event. No eval. No raw SQL from body'; registry webhook.pipeline[9] 'switch-event-no-eval-no-raw-sql'.
findings.code_guidance: try { $data = json_decode($raw, true, 32, JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR); } catch (\JsonException $e) { return $this->deny(); } if (!is_array($data)) { return $this->deny(); }

findings.topic: Cross-session forgery — payload.session, and why the JSON session name is never authentication
findings.answer: ATTACK: a second WAHA session (a test session, another tenant on the same WAHA container, or a compromised staging session that shares the key) posts events naming session 'apollo'; or conversely real 'apollo' events are accepted from a context they should not be. The docs are explicit that 'trust JSON session: apollo' is not security, because anyone can write that string — its value is only as an allowlist AFTER the signature proves the body came from the key holder. Treating a matching session name as a reason to relax any other check inverts the whole model. DEFENCE: compare only after HMAC success; is_string() the value first (it can arrive as an array, int, null or bool); strict === against Apollo_Waha_Options::get('apollo_wa_session','apollo'); absent or mismatched → the same opaque 401. Look in both the documented locations (top-level `session` and `payload.session`) but require the one the spec names rather than accepting whichever happens to match. MISTAKE: `if ($data['session'] == $expected)` (loose), or `if (!empty($data['session']))` (presence, not equality), or skipping the check for session.status 'because status events are harmless'.
findings.evidence: docs/WEBHOOK-SECURITY.md:54 'payload.session must equal option apollo_wa_session. Else drop'; :75 'Trust JSON session: apollo — anyone forges JSON'; registry webhook.pipeline[7] 'session-name-must-match-option'; inc/class-options.php:27 default 'apollo'.
findings.code_guidance: $expected = (string) Apollo_Waha_Options::get('apollo_wa_session', 'apollo'); $got = $data['session'] ?? ($data['payload']['session'] ?? null); if (!is_string($got) || '' === $expected || $got !== $expected) { return $this->deny(); }

findings.topic: The webhook mutating what it must never mutate — queue status / approving a join
findings.answer: ATTACK: an event-driven path that writes queue status turns any signature compromise, any replay, or any WAHA-side bug into unauthorised group membership — the webhook approving a join is exactly the privilege the admin nonce + apollo_manage_whatsapp capability exist to protect. Even without compromise, a retried group.v2.participants event would flip queue rows on WAHA's schedule rather than an operator's. DEFENCE: this run's handler touches nothing but the Session strip; it must not call Apollo_Waha_Queue at all, must not write queue post meta or status, must not fire any action a queue listener consumes, and must not create a CPT or table to 'stage' events. group.v2.participants and message.reaction are acknowledged with 200 and otherwise ignored. Enforce it structurally: no reference to the Queue class exists in the file. MISTAKE: 'while I'm here, mark the queue row added when the participant event arrives' — the single change the registry flags twice as never.
findings.evidence: docs/WEBHOOK-SECURITY.md:90 'Admin composer → nonce + apollo_manage_whatsapp. Webhook never Approves'; :116 audit 'Webhook never changes queue to added/approved'; registry webhook.never_approves_queue=true, security.webhook_never_approves_queue=true; never[]: 'CPT registration outside apollo-core'.
findings.code_guidance: Keep the dispatch switch to case 'session.status' only; default: return 200 with no side effect. No `Apollo_Waha_Queue`, no update_post_meta, no wpdb write anywhere in the file.

findings.topic: Storing message payloads in wp_options — autoload, PII, and the WP_DEBUG gate
findings.answer: ATTACK/FAILURE: 'message may store last payload option for debug' is the most dangerous line in the brief. (a) Autoload: Apollo_Waha_Options::set() passes autoload=false ONLY for the two SECRET_KEYS — any other key is written with autoload TRUE, so the last WhatsApp message (phone number, message text, chat id) is loaded into alloptions on every single page view, front and admin, for every visitor, and is exposed to any plugin that dumps options or any tool that reads the alloptions cache. (b) Personal data at rest: phone numbers and message bodies land in wp_options and therefore in every DB backup, every migration, and every staging clone — an LGPD exposure for a Brazilian site with no retention bound and no deletion path (uninstall.php cannot be edited this run, so an option persists forever after uninstall). (c) The stored blob can also capture headers, and with them the signature. DEFENCE: gate on WP_DEBUG (and prefer a short-TTL transient over an option so it self-expires and needs no uninstall edit); store a redacted, truncated summary — event name, session, message id, byte length — never the body text or the sender number; if an option must be used, call update_option($k, $v, false) directly so autoload is explicitly false; never store headers or the raw body. MISTAKE: `Apollo_Waha_Options::set('apollo_wa_last_webhook', $raw);` — autoloaded PII on every page load, forever.
findings.evidence: inc/class-options.php:17-20 SECRET_KEYS; :43-45 set() → update_option(..., is_secret ? false : true); registry never[] 'secrets in this JSON or front DOM'; files_on_disk lists uninstall.php (not editable this run).
findings.code_guidance: if (defined('WP_DEBUG') && WP_DEBUG) { set_transient('apollo_wa_last_hook', array('event'=>$event,'session'=>$session,'id'=>$msg_id,'bytes'=>strlen($raw)), 15 * MINUTE_IN_SECONDS); } // no body text, no phone, no headers, no signature

findings.topic: Secret leakage — logs, responses, DOM, registry, query strings, stack traces
findings.answer: ATTACK: the key is a bearer credential; one leak makes every later check theatre. Leak paths specific to this file: error_log/wp-content/debug.log lines that print $key, $calc, $sig or $raw (the raw body is itself PII); WP_Error messages and WP_REST_Response bodies, which WordPress serialises straight back to the caller; an uncaught TypeError/ValueError printing a stack trace with arguments while display_errors is on; ever putting a token in the URL (?token= leaks to access logs, CDN logs, Referer headers, and browser history); writing the key or the last payload anywhere a front-end view or wp_localize_script can read; pasting the key into waha-registry.json. DEFENCE: the key is read into a local variable, used once in hash_hmac, and never touched again — not logged, not echoed, not stored, not returned, not compared in a message. Logs record only a category and the sanitised request id. No route or response ever carries a token. Also rate-limit or WP_DEBUG-gate the logging itself: an unauthenticated attacker who can write a log line per request can fill the disk. MISTAKE: a 'temporary' debugging line — `error_log('hmac calc=' . $calc . ' got=' . $sig . ' body=' . $raw);` — which leaks the forgery oracle, the key-equivalent digest, and the customer's phone number in one statement.
findings.evidence: docs/WEBHOOK-SECURITY.md:59 'Never JS, DOM, git, access log'; :74 '?token= leaks in logs / CDN / referrer'; :79 'Log body + hmac key → secret leak'; :112 'Keys never on front'; registry never[] 'secrets in this JSON or front DOM', security.no_token_in_querystring/no_secrets_in_dom; inc/class-options.php:54-63 mask() exists precisely so full values are never printed.
findings.code_guidance: if (defined('WP_DEBUG') && WP_DEBUG) { error_log('apollo-waha webhook denied: ' . $reason_slug . ' id=' . $safe_id); } // slug only: 'no_sig' | 'bad_algo' | 'bad_sig' | 'stale' | 'session' — never $raw, $key, $calc, $sig

findings.topic: 401 must not hint the key was 'almost correct'
findings.answer: ATTACK: differential responses turn the 401 into an oracle. If the body says 'missing signature' vs 'invalid signature' vs 'stale timestamp' vs 'unknown session', an attacker learns which stage they reached and can enumerate: a valid session name, whether their clock trick worked, whether a captured digest is stale rather than wrong. Worse shapes: echoing the expected digest or its first bytes 'for debugging', returning a hint like 'signature differs at position 12', or varying HTTP status (401 vs 403 vs 400) by failure kind. Response timing is a weaker but real side channel — a missing header returns before any hashing while a bad signature returns after. DEFENCE: one WP_Error instance, one message, one status 401, identical body for every authentication failure; the discriminating reason goes to the server-side log only. Accept the small timing difference rather than adding fake delays, but do not amplify it by doing expensive work only on some branches. MISTAKE: `return new WP_Error('bad_hmac', 'HMAC mismatch: expected ' . substr($calc,0,8), ['status'=>401]);`
findings.evidence: docs/WEBHOOK-SECURITY.md:102 '401 must not leak "key almost correct"'; :115 audit '401 does not hint key proximity'; status table :96 groups no-hmac / bad-hmac / bad-algo / stale-ts / bad-session under one code.
findings.code_guidance: A single private deny() returning the same WP_Error for all five failure kinds; the reason slug is a separate argument used only for logging, never placed in the WP_Error message or data.

findings.topic: Type confusion / null / array-vs-string on PHP 8.3
findings.answer: ATTACK: every header and every JSON value is attacker-shaped. In PHP 8.3: hash_equals/hash_hmac throw TypeError on non-string args; (string) on an array yields 'Array' plus a warning rather than failing, so an `event` or `session` sent as ["session.status"] can silently cast into a comparison; (int) on '1.7e12' or 'abc' yields surprising or zero values, and a non-numeric timestamp cast to 0 happens to fail closed but only by luck; array offsets on null emit warnings and produce null; `switch` uses loose comparison, so `switch ($event) { case 'message': }` with $event === 0 or true can match unintended arms. json_decode returning null/true/scalar rather than an array. DEFENCE: is_string()/is_array()/is_numeric() (or ctype_digit) as explicit gates before every use, `match(true)` or a strict switch over an already-validated string, ?? null-coalescing everywhere, and a regex shape check on the hex digest and the request id. MISTAKE: `switch ((string) $data['event'])` — casts arrays, tolerates nulls, and relies on switch's loose compare.
findings.evidence: docs/WEBHOOK-SECURITY.md:56 'Then switch event'; inc/Session/class-session.php:67 already shows the pattern to avoid — strtoupper((string) ($result['body']['status'] ?? '')) casts an array to 'Array'.
findings.code_guidance: $event = $data['event'] ?? null; if (!is_string($event)) { return $this->deny(); } switch ($event) { case 'session.status': …; default: return new WP_REST_Response(null, 200); } // and ctype_digit((string) $ts) before any arithmetic on the timestamp

findings.topic: Raw-body integrity — hash the exact bytes, once
findings.answer: ATTACK/FAILURE: the MAC is over bytes, so any normalisation between the wire and hash_hmac either breaks every request or, worse, lets two different bodies map to one verified string. Specific traps: wp_unslash()/stripslashes() on the body (WordPress slashes superglobals, not php://input — applying it corrupts backslashes in message text); using $request->get_json_params() and re-encoding with wp_json_encode() to 'get the body' (key order, unicode escaping and float formatting all change); using $request->get_body() in one place and file_get_contents('php://input') in another; reading php://input twice (empty on some SAPIs, and always empty for multipart/form-data — an attacker sending multipart makes the server hash '' while PHP still populates $_POST); trusting $_POST at all. DEFENCE: read php://input exactly once at the top of verify(), memoize that exact string on the request object, hash it, and parse that same string — never re-read, never re-encode, never unslash. Because verify() and handle() are two WP calls, memoize per request identity, not in a bare property that a second in-process rest_do_request() could inherit. MISTAKE: verifying file_get_contents('php://input') in verify() and then calling $request->get_json_params() in handle() — the handler acts on data that was never the data you authenticated.
findings.evidence: docs/WEBHOOK-SECURITY.md:48 'Raw body: file_get_contents(php://input). JSON parse AFTER verify'; registry webhook.pipeline[1] 'read-php-input-raw'; WP dispatches permission_callback and callback as two calls on the same WP_REST_Request.
findings.code_guidance: private array $verified = []; … $this->verified[spl_object_id($request)] = $data; // in verify(); handle() reads only that entry and denies if absent — never a bare `private bool $ok`

findings.topic: session.status must not forge a WORKING state into the gate's cache
findings.answer: ATTACK/FAILURE: the Session strip's WORKING gate reads transient apollo_wa_session_ping_{md5(session)} and treats it as a live ping result. If the webhook writes a synthesised array into that key, the webhook becomes an authority on whether sends are allowed — and any future signature weakness, replay, or a stale WAHA event now flips the global send gate open against a session that is actually down (messages fired into a dead session, or the opposite: a transient 'FAILED' event freezing all sends for 30s). It also couples two modules through a cache key, which is the shape the registry's never[] list is guarding against. DEFENCE: prefer invalidation over fabrication — delete the ping transient so the next strip render re-pings WAHA, which stays the single source of truth; and fire the already-registered apollo/whatsapp/session_status action with a small sanitised array (status label string only, no phone numbers, no raw payload) rather than the raw body. If a value must be written, write it with a TTL no longer than the existing 30s PING_TTL and never let a webhook-sourced value be the thing that makes is_working() true. MISTAKE: set_transient('apollo_wa_session_ping_…', ['ok'=>true,'status'=>200,'body'=>['status'=>'WORKING']], 30) from the webhook.
findings.evidence: inc/Session/class-session.php:32 $cache_key = 'apollo_wa_session_ping_' . md5($session); :44 set_transient(..., PING_TTL=30); :55-58 is_working() reads that cache; :21-22 the action apollo/whatsapp/session_status is already bound; :71 on_status() is an empty method this run may not edit; registry never[] 'cache keys / drop-ins'.
findings.code_guidance: $session = (string) Apollo_Waha_Options::get('apollo_wa_session','apollo'); delete_transient('apollo_wa_session_ping_' . md5($session)); do_action('apollo/whatsapp/session_status', array('session'=>$session,'status'=>$label)); // hook family stays apollo/whatsapp/*

findings.topic: HTTPS gate and the X-Forwarded-Proto trap
findings.answer: ATTACK: pipeline step 1 is 'https-prod'. Behind a reverse proxy or Docker (which is how WAHA is deployed here), is_ssl() returns false because PHP sees plain HTTP on the last hop — a naive gate 401s all production traffic. The dangerous fix is worse: honouring $_SERVER['HTTP_X_FORWARDED_PROTO'] inside the plugin, a header any attacker can set, which turns a transport check into an attacker-controlled boolean and invites the same pattern to spread to X-Forwarded-For allowlisting. DEFENCE: treat HTTPS as transport privacy, never as authentication — the HMAC is the authentication. Gate on is_ssl() OR wp_get_environment_type() === 'local'/'development', never on a forwarded header the plugin itself trusts; proxy-protocol trust belongs in wp-config.php, which this run cannot edit, so fail toward 'HMAC still required' rather than toward 'header says https, therefore fine'. MISTAKE: `if ($_SERVER['HTTP_X_FORWARDED_PROTO'] === 'https') { /* trusted */ }`.
findings.evidence: docs/WEBHOOK-SECURITY.md:47 '1. HTTPS in production. LocalWP lab allowed.'; :76 'IP allowlist alone — NAT/Docker moves; HMAC still required'; registry webhook.pipeline[0] 'https-prod'.
findings.code_guidance: $local = function_exists('wp_get_environment_type') && in_array(wp_get_environment_type(), array('local','development'), true); if (!is_ssl() && !$local) { return $this->deny(); } // no forwarded-header branch inside the plugin

findings.topic: Class availability and fatals inside permission_callback
findings.answer: ATTACK/FAILURE: Apollo_Waha_Options is not in the orchestrator's loader — it exists only because class-client.php require_once's it and happens to be loaded first. Any future reorder, or any path that reaches the REST route without the full boot (a plugin that calls rest_do_request early, or apollo-core missing so boot() never runs while some other loader still registers the route), gives 'Class not found' — a fatal 500 inside permission_callback. A fatal is not a 401: it is an unauthenticated attacker crashing a PHP worker, and with display_errors it prints paths and arguments. DEFENCE: guard the dependency in this file the same way class-client.php does, and treat any missing dependency as deny, not as an exception. MISTAKE: assuming load order because it is correct today — the hard constraint forbids editing class-plugin.php, so the guard must live in class-webhook.php.
findings.evidence: inc/class-plugin.php:34-44 loader list omits inc/class-options.php; inc/Client/class-client.php:10-12 guards it with class_exists + require_once; apollo-waha.php:27-30 boot only runs when apollo-core is present.
findings.code_guidance: if (!class_exists('Apollo_Waha_Options', false)) { require_once APOLLO_WAHA_DIR . 'inc/class-options.php'; } // top of class-webhook.php, mirroring the Client

findings.topic: Retry storms and log-flood DoS on unhandled events
findings.answer: ATTACK/FAILURE: WAHA retries on 5xx. If an unknown or unimplemented event (message.any, message.reaction, group.v2.participants this run) returns 500 or throws, WAHA retries it forever and the site DoSes itself with its own integration — and each retry writes a log line. Separately, an unauthenticated attacker POSTing garbage at a route that logs every 401 fills the disk. The registry's 30 events/min/session rate limit, which would blunt both, is not in this run's pipeline, so the residual risk must be acknowledged rather than assumed handled. DEFENCE: acknowledge anything authenticated-but-unhandled with a plain 200 (WAHA stops retrying) and reserve 500 strictly for a handler that genuinely failed and should be retried; gate the deny-path logging behind WP_DEBUG or a counter so unauthenticated traffic cannot write unbounded log volume. MISTAKE: `default: return new WP_REST_Response(['error'=>'unknown event'], 400);` — WAHA treats it as failure and retries.
findings.evidence: docs/WEBHOOK-SECURITY.md:100 '500 (WAHA will retry — handlers must be idempotent)'; :89 'Group flood → 30 events/min/session'; registry webhook.rate_limit = '30 events/min/session' (not in pipeline[] this run).
findings.code_guidance: default: return new WP_REST_Response(array('ok' => true), 200); // authenticated, understood, intentionally ignored

findings.topic: Route immutability, namespace, hook family and storage boundaries
findings.answer: ATTACK/FAILURE: registry never[] is law, and the tempting 'improvements' all violate it — adding a second route for a debug/ping endpoint, moving to a new namespace, adding a GET variant for browser testing (which would make the endpoint reachable by a link and leak anything it returns into Referer/CDN logs), adding an 'args' schema whose sanitize_callback rewrites the body WP hands the callback, registering a CPT or a custom table to persist events, or emitting a hook outside apollo/whatsapp/*. Each either widens the attack surface or breaks the cell contract. DEFENCE: register_rest_route stays byte-identical in namespace ('apollo/v1'), path ('/wa/webhook') and methods ('POST'); the only change inside register_route() is none. No args array that touches the body. No CPT, no dbDelta, no active_plugins write, no mu-plugin require. MISTAKE: adding 'args' with sanitize callbacks to 'validate input' — it mutates the very bytes whose MAC you verified, and can make handle() act on data that differs from what was signed.
findings.evidence: registry never[]: 'new REST namespace outside apollo/v1', 'new hook family outside apollo/whatsapp/*', 'CPT registration outside apollo-core', 'active_plugins mutation', 'force-load / mu top-level require'; registry rest.routes.webhook path '/wa/webhook' method POST; inc/Webhook/class-webhook.php:24-34 current registration.
findings.code_guidance: Leave register_route() exactly as it stands at inc/Webhook/class-webhook.php:24-34; all new code goes into verify(), handle() and private helpers.

findings.topic: Header smuggling, duplicates, and underscore variants
findings.answer: ATTACK: HTTP header names with underscores (X_Webhook_Hmac) map to the same $_SERVER key as their dashed form (HTTP_X_WEBHOOK_HMAC). Under Apache and some proxy chains an attacker-supplied underscore variant can collide with or override the real header; under nginx+FastCGI underscored headers are dropped by default, so behaviour differs per deployment. Duplicate X-Webhook-Hmac headers are joined by WP with ',' (which fails the hex regex — safe), but reading $_SERVER directly instead can pick an unexpected one. DEFENCE: read every header through WP_REST_Request::get_header() so parsing is consistent and canonicalised, never mix it with raw $_SERVER access for the same header, and shape-validate the result so any joined/duplicated value fails closed. MISTAKE: `$sig = $_SERVER['HTTP_X_WEBHOOK_HMAC'] ?? $request->get_header('x_webhook_hmac');` — two sources, attacker picks.
findings.evidence: docs/WEBHOOK-SECURITY.md:13-18 header table; WP_REST_Request canonicalizes header names (lowercase, '-'→'_').
findings.code_guidance: One accessor for all four headers: $request->get_header('x_webhook_hmac' | 'x_webhook_hmac_algorithm' | 'x_webhook_request_id' | 'x_webhook_timestamp'), each is_string()-guarded and regex-shaped.

findings.topic: Timestamp handling details: direction, units, clock skew, numeric shape
findings.answer: ATTACK/FAILURE: X-Webhook-Timestamp is unix milliseconds. Comparing it against time() (seconds) makes every request look ~1.7 trillion units stale and 401s the whole integration; comparing without abs() accepts arbitrarily far-future timestamps, which is the direction an attacker chooses when they want a captured body to stay 'fresh'; non-numeric input cast with (int) lands on 0 and fails closed only by accident; on any 32-bit build a millisecond value exceeds PHP_INT_MAX and silently becomes a float. And because the header is outside the MAC (see the replay finding), the window is spam-shedding, not proof of freshness. DEFENCE: require ctype_digit on the trimmed string, compare in milliseconds against (int) round(microtime(true) * 1000), use abs() so future and past are both bounded by 300000, and document that real freshness comes from the body-derived idempotency key. Server clock drift (no NTP on the host) is the most likely cause of a sudden 100% 401 rate — worth a log slug distinct from 'bad_sig' in the server-side log only. MISTAKE: `if (time() - (int) $ts > 300)` — wrong unit, wrong direction, no shape check.
findings.evidence: docs/WEBHOOK-SECURITY.md:52 '|now_ms - X-Webhook-Timestamp| > 300000 → 401 replay'; :18 'X-Webhook-Timestamp | unix ms'; registry webhook.pipeline[5] 'timestamp-window-300s-401'.
findings.code_guidance: $ts = $request->get_header('x_webhook_timestamp'); if (!is_string($ts) || !ctype_digit(trim($ts))) { return $this->deny(); } if (abs((int) round(microtime(true)*1000) - (int) trim($ts)) > 300000) { return $this->deny(); }

findings.topic: Key reuse across environments, rotation, and object-cache eviction
findings.answer: ATTACK/FAILURE (residual, mostly operational but shaped by this code): (a) if staging and production share apollo_wa_hmac_key, any body signed for staging replays verbatim into production — the session-name check is the only thing standing between them, so staging must use a different session name AND a different key. (b) Rotation has no grace window in this design: changing the key 401s every in-flight WAHA retry; a single-key compare is correct for this run, but the operator must expect a gap. (c) The dedupe transient lives in an external object cache when one is installed, where it can be evicted well before 10 minutes under memory pressure — shrinking the replay window silently; with no persistent cache it lives in wp_options and is bounded by cron cleanup instead. (d) wp_generate_password(48, true, true) emits special characters that docker-compose env interpolation can mangle ($ expansion, quotes), producing a key mismatch that looks exactly like an attack in the logs. DEFENCE: distinct key and session per environment; log the deny slug so 'bad_sig on 100% of traffic' is diagnosable as config, not attack; never widen the window to compensate for cache eviction.
findings.evidence: docs/WEBHOOK-SECURITY.md:36 'hmac.key = same as option apollo_wa_hmac_key'; :40-41 global env fallback; :58 wp_generate_password(48, true, true); registry webhook.transient_prefix; inc/class-options.php:27 session default 'apollo'.
findings.code_guidance: No code change required in this file beyond the distinct deny slugs; treat it as a deployment note attached to the run.

summary:
Threat model for inc/Webhook/class-webhook.php (RUN 2, HMAC only), read-only review of docs/WEBHOOK-SECURITY.md, waha-registry.json (webhook.pipeline[], security{}, never[]) and the current fail-closed stub. 26 findings ranked by severity, each with the attack, the concrete code-level defence, and the specific coding mistake that introduces it.

Six findings are the ones that would actually get exploited and are easy to write wrong:

1. EMPTY KEY (critical, and specific to this repo): apollo_wa_hmac_key defaults to '' (inc/class-options.php:26) and is generated ONLY when an admin saves Tela 1 (admin/class-admin.php:128-129) — never on activation. The route registers unconditionally. Without an explicit emptiness/length gate before hash_hmac, a fresh install signs with the empty string and every attacker can forge. Must reject when the key is not a string or is shorter than 32 bytes (registry hmac_min_bytes), using the same opaque 401.

2. THE TIMESTAMP AND REQUEST-ID ARE OUTSIDE THE MAC (critical design finding): the signature covers raw_body only (docs:21). Both replay defences are unauthenticated headers an attacker rewrites at will — set the timestamp to now to pass the 300s window, randomise the Request-Id to miss the dedupe transient. Neither stops replay of a captured signed body. The dedupe key must be derived from signed material: an id inside the verified payload, falling back to hash('sha256', $raw), optionally combined with (never replaced by) the header id.

3. BARE `return false` GIVES 403, NOT 401: WP converts it via rest_authorization_required_code(), which returns 403 when an auth cookie is present — contradicting the status table and creating an identity oracle on a route that must be identity-blind. Deny must be a WP_Error with an explicit array('status' => 401), one identical instance for all five failure kinds (docs:102, :115 — must not hint the key was almost correct).

4. PIPELINE ORDER IS A DoS TRAP: pipeline[] puts body-max-256kb at position 9, after hash_hmac at position 5. Implemented literally, an unauthenticated 200MB POST is SHA-512'd before the size check. Measure strlen($raw) immediately after reading php://input, before any hashing; never trust Content-Length; never mb_strlen.

5. hash_equals(null, …) THROWS in PHP 8.3: omitting X-Webhook-Hmac produces a TypeError → 500 with a stack trace (potentially carrying the raw body) instead of a 401. Every header needs is_string() plus a shape regex (/^[0-9a-f]{128}$/ for the digest), and no Throwable may escape verify().

6. THE DEBUG PAYLOAD OPTION IS AN AUTOLOADED PII LEAK: Apollo_Waha_Options::set() passes autoload=false only for the two SECRET_KEYS (inc/class-options.php:43-45), so any other key — e.g. a last-webhook debug option — is autoloaded into alloptions on every front and admin page load, permanently, with phone numbers and message text, in every DB backup, with no uninstall path editable this run. Gate on WP_DEBUG, prefer a short-TTL transient over an option, store a redacted summary (event, session, message id, byte length) and never body text, headers or the signature.

Also covered in detail: algorithm confusion (never pass X-Webhook-Hmac-Algorithm into hash_hmac); why ==, ===, strcmp and substr fast-paths are all timing oracles and why no strlen pre-check belongs in front of hash_equals; retry-vs-replay (marking seen before handling silently loses events on 500; get/set is TOCTOU); unsanitised Request-Id concatenated into a 191-char wp_options name (truncation, collision, and the empty-id case that poisons one shared key and drops every event for 10 minutes); JSON depth/JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR plus the absolute ban on unserialize/maybe_unserialize/extract; payload.session as post-HMAC allowlist only, strict === after is_string; the queue-mutation ban enforced structurally (no Queue reference in the file); type confusion on PHP 8.3 (array-to-'Array' casts, loose switch, (int) on timestamps); raw-body integrity (no wp_unslash, no re-encode via get_json_params, read php://input once, memoize per spl_object_id since verify() and handle() are two calls); the session.status handler forging a WORKING ping into apollo_wa_session_ping_{md5} and thereby becoming the authority on the send gate (prefer delete_transient + do_action('apollo/whatsapp/session_status')); is_ssl() behind Docker and the X-Forwarded-Proto trap; Apollo_Waha_Options not being in the orchestrator loader (guard with class_exists + require_once inside class-webhook.php, since class-plugin.php cannot be edited); unhandled events returning 500 causing WAHA retry storms plus log-flood DoS; route/namespace/hook-family immutability and why an 'args' schema would mutate the bytes you authenticated; header underscore smuggling and duplicates; and cross-environment key reuse, rotation gaps, and object-cache eviction shrinking the replay window.

No files were created, edited, or written; no git state was mutated.
